claim.summary: Dedicated specialist research supports chattel slavery in Late Period Egypt before Ptolemaic rule. The documented practices include hereditary enslaved status, resale, leasing and the branding of enslaved persons as property. This corrects older assumptions that chattel slavery was absent before Alexander while still distinguishing Late Period slavery from the larger-scale, commercialized and taxed slavery documented under the Ptolemies.

territorial_practice.notes: P3 reflects multiple institution-defining practices—hereditary status, alienability through resale and leasing, and bodily marking of ownership—identified by dedicated specialist scholarship. It deliberately stops below P4 because the reviewed scholarship emphasizes comparatively scant documentation and explicitly differentiates this system from the larger-scale commercialization of the Ptolemaic period.

source.title: Slavery and Servitude in Late Period Egypt (c. 900–330 BC)
source.independence_notes: Dedicated specialist study based on Egyptian and Aramaic documentation and focused specifically on the nature and extent of slavery and servitude in Late Period Egypt.
source.reliability_limitations: The surviving documentation is scant and uneven. The study distinguishes Late Period slavery from Ptolemaic large-scale commercialized slavery, so evidence of chattel status must not be inflated into a claim that Late Period Egypt was a slave society or that prevalence was uniform.

source.title: ‘Mark them with my Mark’: Human Branding in Egypt
source.independence_notes: Focused philological study of Aramaic and Egyptian textual evidence for marking enslaved persons in Late Period Egypt. It is by the same specialist as the broader synthesis and is therefore not treated as an independent source-count multiplier.
source.reliability_limitations: The article establishes a specific ownership practice rather than population prevalence. Its textual corpus cannot by itself quantify how common slavery was across all of Late Period Egypt.
